title: Half a Minute of Silent Video
text:
In 1993 Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal of Harvard University asked how much people reveal in a few seconds of behavior. They used videotapes of college teaching fellows giving classes. From each tape they cut three ten-second clips, from the beginning, middle and end of a class, and removed the sound.

Students who had never seen these teachers watched the silent clips and rated them on traits such as confident, active, optimistic, warm, enthusiastic and likable. The researchers then compared these ratings with the evaluations the teachers had received from their own students at the end of the semester, after months of classes.

The match was remarkably strong. Judgments from thirty seconds of silent video predicted the end-of-term ratings well. When the clips were cut down further, to two-second slices, the predictions remained surprisingly good. A similar study with high school teachers found the same pattern. Ambady called these brief samples of behavior "thin slices." Gestures, posture, facial expression and energy communicated a great deal about how a teacher would be experienced, before a single word of content could be judged.
lesson: People read your manner within seconds, before they weigh your words. Warmth, energy and attention in how you show up shape how you are received.
source: Ambady, N., and Rosenthal, R. (1993). Half a minute: Predicting teacher evaluations from thin slices of nonverbal behavior and physical attractiveness. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(3), 431-441.
caveat: The samples of teachers were small, and student evaluations themselves reflect impressions more than how much students learn.
